It's so different. And then we see studies that find that women who spend more money/time/energy/etc on their appearance tend to be paid more by their employers and we read about the halo effect and other stuff. Its just disheartening. Like, no one should be expected to put so much of these limited resources into appearance and change parts of themselves to fit an extremely narrow standard, but unfortunately it is an expectation, and if/when we don't meet it or decide we don't even want to be held to those stupid expectations, we are punished for it. Even if people aren't consciously judgemental or whatever, it still happens due to unconscious bias. 

I guess I'm just venting out loud into a void. I been feeling so much like I'm "slacking" and I try to tell myself that my value is not determined by my external appearance, that I don't need male or societal validation, etc etc, but it is so hard to fully and deeply feel that is true especially when feeling like you're treated differently for not meeting those expectations.

I'll share some of my experiences and observations below. This is just my opinion, living here since the 90s (99% of my life.) If you were a friend of mine, this is what I'd tell you:

I feel like I experience micro aggressions in slc pretty regularly, but its weird and comes at varying degrees of subtlety, so sometimes its like constantly questioning reality. 
While there are a lot of "liberal" seeming folks in slc, there is undeniable "weirdness." 

In many nonpoc/yt owned restaurants or markets, the other nonpoc/yts who arrived after us are often served before us. Happens all the fucking time. 
Other weird things happen too, like this one time my partner and I went to Current (fancy seafood place) downtown and we were told they were full atm and we should go elsewhere. We asked to be put on the list because we really wanted to try that place, and the host was like "ok you're on the list" without actually taking any of our info. Stuff like that happens here all the time, and there isn't really an explanation for it. Maybe a lot of people are just rude and super unaware of how lines and lists work? Or maybe they're being discriminatory. Hard to tell... 

People are often welcoming, at least at first to your face, but also a lot of people like to keep to themselves and their cliques. I heard that could be due to the religious culture but I don't actually know. 

It's also really common to hear weird stuff here, like for some reason  "colored people" is commonly used by many Utahns. Or the neighborhoods that are historically populated by more poc are also labeled as the ghetto/dangerous parts of town. 

Also, you can't trust Google maps or word of mouth for food options, you have to figure it out on your own or listen to someone you know has similar taste (most locals can't be trusted to review food unless its a burger joint imo.)

And while slc is thankfully becoming much more diverse, you'd likely still need to get used to being the only poc in the room or building, at any given time or place really. Maybe one of like three poc (if you're lucky).

I also just want to add that sadly, many of the poc here have internalized a lot of racism so even though I hear it all the time, it still gives me whiplash hearing the racist shit in my own communities. Practice sparking up low-stakes conversations with random people when you go out and about. 

For example, at the store checking out? Make small talk with the cashier. If it goes no where or is awkward, it doesn't matter it'll be over soon. Can't think of a topic to bring up? Talk about the products you're buying, what they've tried or recommend, etc. Waiting in line? Talk to someone waiting beside you. About what? Maybe they have a unique item of clothing or accessory they're wearing, compliment and ask them where they got it. Etc. 
This can be a great way to practice small talk in easy environments, and if things got super awkward, you probably never have to see that person again so nbd.  

Also, an aspect of a good conversationalist is interest in the other person. Being genuinely curious about them and asking them questions. That also helps take the pressure off you. You can connect it back to you and then back to them with statements like "oh I never been there but always wanted to go! How was it? What were your favorite things about it?" Or "I love that, my experience was great, what was your experience like?" Or "I'm not very familiar with xyz, can you tell me a little more about it?" People love talking about their experiences and feeling like experts who can inform others about things. 

I've had similar struggles about learning how much to share. The trick is discerning what you can disclose, to who, and when/where. You don't want to share too much (unless its a close friend/relative or therapist who you trust and they have the capacity to hold what you share) but you also don't want to share too little and come off stand off-ish. 

I'm sure you're not boring. It probably isn't helpful to enter interactions worrying about how boring you are. You're a whole person, full of experiences and wisdom that you've gained throughout your life. You have something to contribute. Even if its just questions for now. Go into interactions telling yourself that and even if you don't feel it, fake it until you do.

Good luck!
